opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. One thing I've learned from building a lot of startups at AI Fund is that concrete ideas are much easier to execute on than vague ones. If someone comes to me and says, "Let's use AI to improve healthcare," that's a nice sentiment, but it's not actionable. There's no way for an engineer to go and write code for that. But if someone says, "Let's build software that helps hospitals schedule MRI machines more efficiently so patients wait less," now that's concrete. An engineer can start building, you can go talk to customers, and you can quickly find out whether it's a good idea or a bad one.

And that's really the key: with a concrete idea, you get feedback fast. Maybe it turns out to be wrong, and that's fine, because you learn that quickly and pivot. With a vague idea, it's never wrong, because it's never specific enough to be tested. Teams can spend months debating and not make progress.

The other thing is that concrete ideas usually come from someone who has thought deeply about a problem, often a subject matter expert who has lived with it for a long time. Those people tend to have surprisingly good instincts about what will work. So when I see a concrete idea, it often signals that someone has done the hard thinking already, and that lets the team move fast. In the AI era, speed matters a lot, especially now that AI coding tools make prototyping so much faster. The bottleneck is shifting toward deciding what to build, and being concrete is what unlocks that speed.

r001.rationale: It says concreteness makes an idea actionable and testable, while acknowledging that a concrete idea may still turn out to be wrong.

r002.rationale: It explains that a concrete idea lets the team talk to customers and quickly learn whether it is a good idea.

r003.rationale: It says engineers can start building and prototype faster, but does not clearly explain that concreteness helps assess technical feasibility.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so one of the things we've learned at AI Fund is that concrete ideas are just much easier to validate and execute on. If someone comes to me and says, "let's use AI to improve healthcare," that sounds exciting, but it's so vague that a team could spend months and not really know whether they're making progress. Whereas if someone says, "let's build a tool that automatically fills out prior authorization forms for a specific type of clinic," that's something we can go test next week. We can talk to ten clinics, show them a mockup, and find out pretty quickly whether this is a real pain point.

The other thing is that a concrete idea lets the whole team move fast, because everyone knows what to build. Vague ideas tend to generate a lot of debate, and the engineers end up waiting around for the direction to get clarified. With a concrete spec, I can hand it to a small team and they just go.

Now, the obvious objection is, what if the concrete idea is wrong? And honestly, a lot of them are. But I think being concretely wrong is actually fine, because you find out fast and you can pivot. Being vaguely right is much worse, because you never get the signal that tells you what to do next. So I'd rather commit to a specific idea, run the experiment, and let the market correct us, than sit in a conference room for six months trying to figure out the perfect thing to build.

r001.rationale: The response says many concrete ideas are wrong but can be tested and corrected quickly, distinguishing concreteness from idea quality.

r002.rationale: It explains that a specific idea can be tested quickly with clinics and a mockup to learn whether it addresses a real customer pain point.

r003.rationale: The response says a concrete spec helps a team know what to build and move quickly, but it does not explain assessing whether the idea is technically feasible.

astra-6.text:
At AI Fund, I find that the more concrete an idea is, the faster we can validate it. “Let’s use AI to improve healthcare” is a worthy aspiration, but it doesn’t tell a team what to build or whom to talk to. “Let’s help a hospital predict which patients will miss an appointment”—now we can ask specific questions. Does someone need this? Is the data available? Can we build something accurate enough to be useful? And who would pay for it?

Being concrete doesn’t mean we’re certain the idea is right. It means we can discover quickly where we’re wrong. We can talk to potential customers, build a prototype, and revise the idea based on what we learn. That gives a team a much clearer path forward than spending months exploring a broad theme.

r001.rationale: It says being concrete does not mean the idea is right, distinguishing concreteness from whether it is good.

r002.rationale: It explains that a specific idea lets the team quickly ask whether anyone needs it and talk to potential customers.

r003.rationale: It explains that a specific idea lets the team assess data availability and whether they can build something accurate enough to be useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I find that with AI, the details really matter. If someone says, “Let’s use AI in health care,” that’s a huge area, but it’s hard to know what to do next. If instead they say, “Let’s help a hospital automate this particular administrative workflow,” we can ask concrete questions: Can we build it? Who’s the customer? How much value does it create? Will someone pay for it?

A concrete idea gives you something you can test. It doesn’t mean the initial idea is right. But you can talk to customers, build a prototype, and learn quickly. I’d much rather start with a specific hypothesis and revise it than spend months discussing an opportunity in the abstract.

r001.rationale: It says a concrete idea does not mean the initial idea is right, distinguishing specificity from whether the idea is good.

r002.rationale: It says a concrete idea can be tested by talking to customers and asking who the customer is and whether someone will pay.

r003.rationale: It identifies technical feasibility questions—“Can we build it?”—and mentions building a prototype.
